paras: The Riverside Park attack was an assault by a gang of white youths known as the "Bungaloos" on Black visitors to Riverside Park in Indianapolis, Indiana, on the night of Sunday, June 7, 1903. Gang members picketed the street-car lines, kept Black passengers on the cars and stoned Black people who took refuge in them, striking several people. No arrests were reported, but the attack led city park and police officials to post patrolmen in the parks, and both the white Indianapolis Journal and the Black Indianapolis Freeman called for action against "Bungalooism."

According to a June 14 dispatch to the New York Sun, a "Bungaloo" gang organized among "white toughs" two years earlier had attacked Black people who used the city parks during the previous season, and many Black youths had armed themselves in response. The Journal later wrote that the original gang had long since broken up but that the name survived as "a rallying cry for any crowd of rowdies," and that attacks on Black residents were frequent, especially in the northwestern part of the city. The Freeman noted that the "Bungaloo" question had been an issue in the last municipal campaign and that the city administration had promised Black residents protection.

On the night of June 7 the gang "turned out in full force" at Riverside Park, according to the Journal, posting pickets at the street-car lines; within minutes no Black person could be found near the grounds. Black people caught inside the park fled to the street cars, where a crowd the Journal called a "howling mob of whites" pelted them with stones and rocks. Several people were struck by bricks and stones and a number of doctors were summoned; the coverage gives no names or count of the injured.

Police Captain Kruger sent twelve policemen and four detectives to the park, and the trouble soon subsided. The attackers dispersed once they learned the police had been called, and none were found or arrested.

The next day Superintendent of Parks J. Clyde Power announced a campaign against "hoodlums," calling the Sunday night "outrage" the "last straw," and stationed two patrolmen at Riverside with orders to arrest known gang members at the slightest disorder. Mayor Bookwalter and the police chief pledged him their support, and Superintendent Taffe told his men to watch the gang.

On June 14, after the police heard of a planned "Bungaloo" disturbance, one hundred special policemen were sworn in to guard Riverside, Fairview, Garfield and Military parks; many Black residents went to the parks that evening prepared to defend themselves, but no violence followed. Later in June the Journal reported additional sergeants and orders for prompt action against "hoodlum tactics," while the Freeman reported that Judge Whallon had fined two armed Black youths bound for Riverside Park and promised to punish both the "bungaloos" and those who went armed to hunt them. No report of arrests or prosecutions for the June 7 attack was found.

The Indianapolis Journal broke the story on June 8 under the headline "Hoodlums Out in Force," with the deck "Bungaloos Attack Peaceable Negroes at Riverside Park." Its account treated the Black victims as "unfortunate negroes" and the attackers as "miscreants," and the next day the paper both reported the officials' response and urged in an editorial paragraph that sending a few gang members to the penitentiary would have "a very wholesome effect." Its later editorial on "Bungalooism" called the participants "irresponsible boys in their later 'teens" and stressed that the gangs did not attack Black people alone.

The Indianapolis Freeman, a Black weekly, addressed the attack in a June 13 editorial paragraph that described "a gang of white boys" who set out to "make it warm for the colored boys." Citing witnesses and the daily papers, it judged the gang "bent on mischief from the start" and framed the episode as a test of the city administration's campaign promise to protect Black residents. The Freeman gave no details of the stoning, and its later items noted the mayor's pledge against "Bungaloolism" and cautioned Black youths against going out armed.

accounts.gist: The Bungaloo gang picketed the car lines, kept Black passengers on the cars and stoned those who sheltered in them; several people were hurt, police arrived and the gang dispersed without arrests.

accounts.label: Freeman editorial
